https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/09/2.text: Not-so-fun (but interesting) fact: The U.S. spends more on servicing its debt (about 15% of the overall budget) than on defense (about 13%), and it's been that way since 2024. Even if it isn't the biggest line item on the overall U.S. budget, this country allocates a mammoth amount of money to military and national security spending. Earlier this year, the White House unveiled its fiscal 2027 defense budget request, and it totaled a staggering $1.5 trillion, a 42% increase over 2026. That's just a single year's budget request. Clearly, this country spends big on defense. Global governments are accelerating defense spending. Image source: Getty Images. And the United States isn't the only country spending more on defense. Other countries are boosting defense expenditures significantly in response to the ongoing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, out of a desire to be proactive, to spur economic activity, or for other reasons. Global defense spending reached a jaw-dropping $2.9 trillion last year, accounting for roughly 2.5% of the world's economic output. When category spending approaches $3 trillion annually, there is a range of investment implications to consider . Some of the more compelling defense spending investment opportunities arrive courtesy of the largest industrial companies by market cap , including Honeywell Aerospace ( HONA +2.55% ) and RTX ( RTX +0.90% ) . A big backlog and more RTX is getting so many business requests that it now has a sizable backlog of $289 billion, and, even more impressively, it could surge to $460 billion by the end of 2028. Clearly, RTX has become a preferred defense vendor for various governments, including the U.S. RTX is also positioned as a prime beneficiary of an expected U.S. military replenishment cycle. While accounts vary, the U.S. has used up a significant amount of its ordinance in the war in Iran. For example, it now has a dwindling supply of the critical Tomahawk missile, produced by RTX. To help manage supply, the U.S. indefinitely halted shipments of Tomahawk missiles to Japan back in May. And this summer, the U.S. spent nearly $23 billion to entice RTX to accelerate Tomahawk production. Being in demand by the U.S. government is an enviable position for securing defense contracts and supports the long-term RTX investment thesis. But RTX is also in demand by other governments. The aforementioned Japan is ramping up military spending and could soon raise it to 3.5% of the country's GDP (up from 2% in 2025). I was on the pothole crew in the summer of 1978. I just graduated from high school and secured a summer job before I headed off to college. My crew was mostly older men who had been there for years. Their tools were heavy-duty rakes, shovels and steam rollers. Young guys like me were given the more strenuous job and put at the end of the shovel, digging into a dump truck of black asphalt and learning to “sling” it just right. Slinging involved a sideways motion spreading asphalt evenly so the rakers, with their overalls, T-shirts and steel-toed boots wouldn’t have to expend extra energy raking the “pile” of asphalt you did not “sling” correctly. If you screwed up, old George was on your case. He was of Polish decent and had a bit of an accent. His friends said he was one of the only Poles in St. Paul who could dance the mazurka, an old Polish dance that was part polka and part Virginia reel. Brittanica describes the mazurka as a “Polish folk dance for a circle of couples, characterized by stamping feet and clicking heels and traditionally danced to the music of a village band. The music is in 3/4 or 3/8 time with a forceful accent on the second beat. The dance, highly improvisatory, has no set figures, and more than 50 different steps exist.” George never demonstrated the mazurka for the street crew as he mostly stuck to the back and forth monotonous movement of raking asphalt. At the end of the day, you could get the tar off your boots by going to the large pile of sand heated up by the daytime sun in the asphalt plant yard. You rubbed your boots in the hot sand and the tar melted off. Clean as can be. Of course, 1978 was the year of the Minnesota massacre, when voters resoundingly threw out Democrats in all manner of office, for what I remember my union-member father saying was “arrogance.” Icons like former Gov. Wendall Anderson (who was appointed by his Lt. Gov. Rudy Perpich after he resigned to fill Walter Mondale’s seat) lost in a landslide to GOP businessman Rudy Boschwitz. Independent Republican Dave Durenberger was also elected to the Senate. Politics is unreliable to solve long-term problems at times like filling potholes. You know the temporary fix will smooth the street for a while, but they’ll be back, causing bumps in the road, broken axels and blown tires. It seems like temporary fixes in politics are more likely than not. We don’t have time to do things right. And if we did, who could we blame? Government, of course, and government workers take a lot of blame for things that don’t work. But they rarely get credit for things that do work, like good roads. The act of building a road or completely reconstructing one should allow us to pause for a minute and appreciate the teamwork, the coordination and the steam rollers that brought that road to life. We all may be going different places, but that road gets us there just the same. And we’re more free because of it. Asphalt shovelers, concrete workers, budget planners, accountants and contractors all had a role in the simple act of helping us to conveniently get where we want to go. Ride into the sunset or beat the thunderstorm. We should be thankful. And we should thank those elected leaders who argued with their colleagues for road funding. And had to compromise at times. The city of Mankato and the Minnesota Department of Transportation recently gave us the gift of a new and improved Veterans Memorial Bridge, a magnificent looking structure that connects the divergent native populations of Mankato and North Mankato. The residents of the two cities may have differences but the thousands of cubic yards of concrete now bridges the divide. And MnDOT recently completed a $37 million project in reconstructing Highway 22 from Mankato to St. Peter, again uniting the people in commerce and culture. A bike trail will lead you to the winery. These are things we should not take for granted. And they are things we must hold up as an accomplishment we achieved together. A new road should not be a partisan issue. Let’s hope that idea can apply elsewhere, like healthcare, poverty and education. We have more things that unite us than divide us. We travel roads together more than we think. We may occasionally need to rub the tar off our boots in the hot sand. But let’s also think about learning the mazurka. Joe Spear is editor emeritus of The Free Press.
